conceptTag: Why airlines match each other's fares
readerTitle: Three airlines, one fare: why prices move together
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (항공권 검색 화면에서 같은 노선 운임이 비슷하게 움직이는 현상) + 가상 적용 (골판지 상자 제조사, 청구서 소프트웨어). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격을 따라 맞출지는 경쟁사의 행동이 아니라 두 가지 조건으로 판단한다. 고객 눈에 내 상품이 상품(commodity)처럼 보이는가, 그리고 시장에 서로를 지켜보는 판매자가 몇 명뿐인가.
misconception: 경쟁사가 가격을 내리면 무조건 따라 내리거나 더 내려야 한다. 또는 운임이 똑같으면 항공사끼리 몰래 담합한 것이다.

sources.text: 과점과 상품화 시장의 표준 경제학 개념 (가격 투명성, 상호 의존적 가격 결정)
US v. Airline Tariff Publishing Co. 외 (미국 법무부, 1992년 제소, 1993~1994년 동의 판결)
모든 수치(운임, 할인율)는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 미국 법무부가 1990년대 초 주요 항공사들이 공동 운임 공시 시스템(ATPCO)으로 가격 신호를 주고받았다고 제소했고, 항공사들은 잘못을 인정하지 않고 동의 판결로 합의했다는 내용입니다. 연도와 합의 방식을 게시 전 1차 자료로 확인하세요.
"같은 노선 운임이 비슷하게 움직인다"는 일반적 관찰로만 썼습니다. 특정 항공사, 특정 노선의 수치나 대응 속도는 쓰지 않았습니다.
가상 수치 확인: $189 → $149는 $40 인하(약 21%). 상자 제조사 8% 할인 제안은 설명용입니다. 계산이 필요한 다른 수치는 없습니다.
경쟁사와 가격을 논의하는 것이 불법이라는 문장은 일반적 원칙으로만 썼습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 표현을 유지하세요.

cards.title: Three airlines, one fare
body: You search for a Friday morning flight. Three airlines fly the route. All three show **$189**.
Next week you search again. One airline has dropped to $149. By the afternoon, the other two show $149 as well.
It looks like a coincidence or a secret deal. Usually it's neither.

image.label: Flight search screen with three identical fares
image.brief: 휴대폰 항공권 검색 화면 일러스트. 서로 다른 색의 가상 항공사 세 곳이 나란히 있고 모두 "$189". 실제 항공사 로고, 이름, 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A rival just cut the fare.
body: You run one of three airlines on this route. Your fare is $189. A rival drops to $149 for the same days and times.
Travelers compare all three on one screen. What do you do?

options.text: Match $149 quickly on the same flights
options.feedback: You protect your bookings, and the rival gains no customers from cutting. With only a few sellers watching each other, a quick match makes the next cut less tempting. That's oligopoly logic.

options.text: Hold $189 and promote your better legroom
options.feedback: Some travelers will pay for comfort. But on a screen sorted by price, most see seats as interchangeable, so you may fly emptier planes.

options.text: Undercut to $129 to win the route
options.feedback: You may win a few days of bookings. Then rivals match again, and everyone flies at $129 for good. A short gain can start a long price war.

cards.title: To a price shopper, a seat is a commodity.
body: A **commodity** is a product buyers see as the same, whoever sells it. Then price decides almost everything.
Most airline seats aren't truly identical. But on a search screen, a Friday 8 a.m. seat looks a lot like a Friday 8:30 a.m. seat. Prices are public and update constantly.
So a $40 gap doesn't last. The cheaper airline fills up and the others empty out, and they all notice within hours.

cards.title: Few sellers means every move is watched.
body: On most routes, only a handful of airlines compete. That is an **oligopoly**: a market with few sellers, where each one's price depends on what the others do.
In a market with hundreds of sellers, nobody reacts to your cut. Here, everyone does. If cuts are matched fast, cutting wins no customers and only lowers everyone's income.
So fares often end up moving together, without anyone talking to anyone.

image.label: Three sellers connected by watching arrows
image.brief: 가상 비행기 세 대(로고 없음)가 삼각형으로 배치되고, 서로를 향한 눈 모양 화살표로 연결. 가운데에 가격표 "$149" 하나. 차분한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Matching is fine. Agreeing is not.
body: Reading a rival's public price and choosing to match it is normal competition. Discussing prices with rivals, or using signals to coordinate them, is illegal in many countries.
In the early 1990s, US regulators accused major airlines of using their shared fare-publishing system to signal price moves. The airlines settled without admitting wrongdoing.
Matching also has a cost: if customers truly prefer you, matching gives away money you didn't need to lose.

cards.title: Now you make cardboard boxes.
body: You are one of three box makers within delivery distance of a large warehouse district. Your biggest customer says a rival offered them **8% less**.
To this buyer, a box is a box. What do you do?

options.text: Confirm the offer is real, then match it for this customer only
options.feedback: The product is close to a commodity, so you likely lose the account if you don't match. Keeping it to one customer avoids handing the cut to everyone, which in an oligopoly invites rivals to cut again.

options.text: Cut your list price 10% for every customer
options.feedback: You win the comparison today, but the other two makers see it and respond. Three sellers watching each other usually ends with everyone at the lower price.

options.text: Refuse and point to your print quality
options.feedback: Right if this buyer truly values print. For plain shipping boxes, they likely see you as interchangeable and will switch.

cards.title: A rival halves its starter plan.
body: Your invoicing software is one of four serious options for small agencies. A rival cuts its starter plan in half.
Your users have years of client records and custom templates in your tool. What do you do?

options.text: Halve your starter plan the same day
options.feedback: This treats you like a commodity seller. Your users face real switching costs, so you'd give up revenue on many accounts to protect a few.

options.text: Hold your price and watch new sign-ups and churn for a month
options.feedback: Few rivals still means you should watch closely. But stored data makes you less of a commodity, so you can wait for evidence before matching.

options.text: Launch a stripped-down plan at the rival's new price
options.feedback: It catches price-shoppers without cutting your main plan. The cost is a new plan to support, and some current users may downgrade.

cards.title: Match when buyers see you as the same and rivals are few.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Commodities:** when buyers can't tell sellers apart, price gaps close fast. **Oligopolies:** when a few sellers watch each other, a quick match makes cutting pointless.
When customers do see a difference, matching gives money away.
**Try it today:** name your two closest rivals. If one cut prices 20% tomorrow, how many of your customers would actually notice and switch?
